title: BlueQubit Benchmarks Quantum Computational Advantage in Random-Circuit Sampling on IBM Nighthawk r2 Hardware - Quantum Computing Report
gist: BlueQubit with EPFL and the XPRIZE Foundation claim quantum computational advantage via random-circuit sampling on 61 qubits of IBM's 120-qubit ibm_phoenix (Nighthawk r2), run through standard Qiskit Runtime cloud queues: 10^6 samples in 19 seconds of QPU time versus an estimated ~110 years on Frontier. The article cautions that the classical baseline assumes exact contractions and could fall with better classical algorithms, as happened with Sycamore and Zuchongzhi.

themes.theme: Advantage claim on commercial cloud hardware

insights.claim: BlueQubit, EPFL and the XPRIZE Foundation report a random-circuit-sampling quantum advantage demonstration on 61 active qubits of IBM's 120-qubit ibm_phoenix processor (Nighthawk r2 square-lattice architecture) using native CZ gates.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Advantage-class RCS is now reproducible by a third party on IBM commercial hardware, not just in-house labs.

insights.claim: The circuits were submitted through standard Qiskit Runtime cloud queues without bespoke hardware calibration, highlighting commercial reproducibility of the result.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cloud-accessible advantage strengthens IBM's commercial positioning versus lab-only demonstrations.
insights.quote: the circuits were submitted through standard Qiskit Runtime cloud queues without bespoke hardware calibration

insights.claim: The ibm_phoenix processor collected 10^6 samples in 19 seconds of QPU time, while tensor-network rejection sampling on ORNL's Frontier supercomputer would need an estimated 1.2 x 10^27 FLOPs, roughly 110 years of exascale compute.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Headline quantum-vs-classical gap is about 11 orders of magnitude in wall time under the stated assumptions.

insights.claim: At the 36-cycle anchor depth (918 CZ gates), where tensor-network contraction cost saturates at full system size with width w = 64, measured fidelity was F_XEB ~ 2.3 x 10^-3.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Advantage was achieved at very low but statistically verified fidelity.
insights.locator: At the anchor depth of 36 cycles

insights.claim: Estimated Frontier rejection-sampling runtime for 10^6 samples rises steeply with depth: 44 seconds at 20 cycles, 2.2 hours at 24, 87 days at 28, 2 years at 32, and about 110 years at 36 cycles.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Classical hardness crosses from seconds to centuries within a 16-cycle window, showing how sharp the advantage boundary is.

insights.claim: Fidelity was established across depths of 4 to 40 cycles using two independent methods, mirror benchmarking with randomized compiling and multi-partition cross-entropy benchmarking, rather than relying solely on extrapolation.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Dual verification addresses the main critique of earlier RCS claims that relied on extrapolated fidelities.
insights.locator: Rather than relying solely on extrapolation

insights.claim: Classical 'severing attacks' that delete cross-boundary couplers all scored below 2.2 x 10^-4 at 36 cycles, at least an order of magnitude below the experimental score, placing the benchmark on the classically hard side of the noise-induced phase transition.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Known XEB spoofing routes do not explain the result.

insights.claim: Per-cycle fidelity on IBM Nighthawk r2 reached 0.872 versus 0.836 on the first-generation Nighthawk r1 (ibm_miami), compounding to more than an order-of-magnitude fidelity gain at deep circuit depths.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Small per-cycle improvements compound into large deep-circuit gains; IBM's hardware cadence is materially improving capability.

insights.so_what: Advantage claims should be discounted for classical-algorithm progress risk.
